VIDEO.title: If Grace Covers Sin… Why Stop Sinning?
VIDEO.series: The Book of Romans, Every Word (playlist of 28 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Romans 5:12-6:2 · Episode 9 (#9 of 28 in the playlist)
hand: Two reigns: sin in death, grace to life
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Romans 5:12-6:2. Sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and death spread to all (5:12). Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even before the Law, and Adam is a type of the One to come (5:13-14). The gift is not like the transgression: through one man's disobedience the many were appointed sinners; through the obedience of the One the many will be appointed righteous (5:15-19). The Law came in so that transgression would increase, 'but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more' (5:20-21). So, are we to continue in sin? 'May it never be!' (6:1-2).

Paul repeats himself on purpose. Sin was the topic in 1:18-32, 2:12, 3:9 and 3:23, each time for a different purpose. Paul, an ex-Pharisee, writes in a Hebraic spiral rather than a straight line: 'braiding' theology. Now sin is not only something we do but a power that reigns, with death as its domain.

Why did death reign before Sinai? Because sin was a real enslaving power long before Torah. Torah defines and reckons sin within the Sinai covenant; it was never meant to make anyone righteous (3:20). 'Sin is not imputed when there is no law' (5:13).

Paul is fixated on Adam, with layers. Genesis 2:17 and 3:19 lie behind 5:12. 'From Adam until Moses' suggests Israel as a corporate Adam: placed in the land like Adam in the garden, priests to 'cultivate and keep,' failing and exiled. Hosea 6:7: 'like Adam they have trespassed against the covenant.' The teacher recommends G. K. Beale's The Temple and the Church's Mission.

One can stand for the many: Aaron atones for all Israel (Leviticus 16:17); the Servant bears the sin of many (Isaiah 53:11-12); 'Israel has sinned' when Achan sinned (Joshua 7:11). Some call this federal headship. Condemnation and justification are courtroom words (Deuteronomy 25:1). In 5:15 and 5:20 Paul argues lesser to greater (qal vahomer): grace does not merely match sin; it overwhelms it.

The lesson: 'Christians live in a world where sin reigns, but they must not live as if sin reigns over them.' The two reigns live side by side, like the wheat and the weeds (Matthew 13:29-30). This is 'not about perfection' but 'about perception': when God's people forget who reigns, they treat one another with suspicion, comparison and judgment.
QUOTES: Christians live in a world where sin reigns, but they must not live as if sin reigns over them.
This is not about perfection. This is about perception.
That kind of behavior does not come from grace reigning, it comes from forgetting who reigns.
Paul wants us to live our faith like we actually believe it's true.

method.p: In Romans 5:12-21 circle every 'reign' or 'reigned' and note who or what reigns: death, sin, grace, believers. Then underline each 'much more.' You will see Paul's two kingdoms and his lesser-to-greater argument.

For as through the one man’s disobedience the many were appointed sinners, even so through the obedience of the One the many will be appointed righteous.

left.text: Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, because all sinned—

right.text: but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it; for in the day that you eat from it you will surely die.”

lines.text: 'Therefore' builds on 5:1-11: why is the victory of grace so sweet? Because of the pervasive power of sin and death that grace has overcome.
Paul has in view both the fall (Genesis 3:6) and God's warning before it, and Adam's sentence: 'For you are dust, and to dust you shall return' (Genesis 3:19).

ADAM.title: Death reigned from Adam until Moses

src.text: for until the Law sin was in the world, but sin is not imputed when there is no law. Nevertheless death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the trespass of Adam, who is a type of Him who was to come.

lines.text: If there was no Torah before Sinai, why were people dying? Because sin was a real enslaving power, and death its domain, long before Torah. Torah defines and reckons sin within the Sinai covenant; it cannot stop or redeem it (Romans 3:20).
Before, the focus was sin as something we do. Now it is sin as a power that reigns.

left.text: But like Adam they have trespassed against the covenant; / There they have dealt treacherously against Me.

right.text: Then Yahweh God took the man and set him in the garden of Eden to cultivate it and keep it.

lines.text: Why 'from Adam until Moses' and not 'until Christ'? The teacher: Israel is portrayed as a corporate Adam. Placed in Canaan as Adam was in Eden; priests to work and keep the sanctuary as Adam was to cultivate and keep the garden; disobedient again and again; exiled as Adam was.
That is why Jesus' life replays and fulfills both Adam's story and Israel's, a theme of the Matthew study. For more, the teacher recommends G. K. Beale, The Temple and the Church's Mission.

left.text: But the gracious gift is not like the transgression. For if by the transgression of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one Man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many.

right.text: Now when he goes in to make atonement in the holy place, no one shall be in the tent of meeting until he comes out, that he may make atonement for himself and for his household and for all the assembly of Israel.

lines.text: Where does Paul get the idea that one man can represent the many? From the Old Testament. Aaron, the high priest, makes atonement for all Israel.
Paul uses qal vahomer again, as in 5:9-11: if death spread to all through one, much more can God's people rest assured that the grace of Christ leads to righteousness and eternal life.

left.text: “Israel has sinned, and they have also trespassed against My covenant which I commanded them. And they have even taken some of the things devoted to destruction and have both stolen and dealt falsely. Moreover, they have also put them among their own things.

right.text: So then as through one transgression there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness there resulted justification of life to all men.

lines.text: Achan stole from the spoils of Jericho, yet God says 'Israel has sinned.' Once again the one stands in for the many. Some today call this federal headship.
The Servant shows the hopeful side: 'He Himself bore the sin of many' (Isaiah 53:12).

left.text: And the gift is not like that which came through the one who sinned; for on the one hand the judgment arose from one transgression resulting in condemnation, but on the other hand the gracious gift arose from many transgressions resulting in justification.

right.text: “If there is a dispute between men and they go to court for judgment, and the judges judge their case, and they justify the righteous and condemn the wicked,

lines.text: Justification is God counting a person righteous, not on the basis of their own works but on the basis of the righteousness of Christ (Romans 3:23-25). God did the same in the past: Genesis 15 and Psalm 32.

src.text: Now the Law came in so that the transgression would increase, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, even so grace would reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

lines.text: Notice the different verbs: sin 'increased' (pleonazō), grace 'abounded all the more,' superabounded. Not both getting bigger, but grace decisively overwhelming sin.
The Law did not force people to sin; it made sin multiply in visibility and accountability so that grace could overwhelm it.

REIGN.title: Are we to continue in sin?

left.text: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin so that grace may increase? May it never be! How shall we who died to sin still live in it?

right.text: And why not say (as we are slanderously reported and as some claim that we say), “Let us do evil that good may come”? Their condemnation is just.

lines.text: Paul spirals back to the objection of chapter 3 because he has just linked increasing sin and abounding grace. He meets the same objection on a deeper level.
Underneath the 'dumb question' is a casual attitude: if sin and grace live so close together, what's the big deal about sin? Is holiness that important?

left.text: But he *said, ‘No; for while you are gathering up the tares, you may uproot the wheat with them. Allow both to grow together until the harvest; and in the time of the harvest I will say to the reapers, “First gather up the tares and bind them in bundles to burn them up; but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”

right.text: so that, as sin reigned in death, even so grace would reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

lines.text: The kingdom of heaven spreads among people beholden to a different kingdom. The parable does not minimize sin; it emphasizes God's patience until the final separation. Those under the reign of grace are constantly surrounded by those under the reign of sin.

TERMS.def: Kingly rule. Paul personifies death, sin and grace as kings (Romans 5:14, 17, 21).
A person or event that prefigures a greater one; Adam is 'a type of Him who was to come' (Romans 5:14).
Counted or charged to someone's account; 'sin is not imputed when there is no law' (Romans 5:13).
The idea that one representative acts for many, as Adam for humanity and Christ for His people.
The video's term for Israel retracing Adam's vocation and failure (Hosea 6:7).
Lesser-to-greater argument: if one man's sin did this, much more will Christ's grace (Romans 5:15, 17).
The judge's verdict of guilty and its sentence; the opposite of justification (Romans 5:16, 18).

BACKGROUND.p: The video describes Paul's style as Hebraic and spiral: he returns to sin, Law and grace again and again, each time with a new purpose. Ancient writers often used repetition and ring structure to build an argument.

Genesis 2:15 says the man was set in the garden 'to cultivate it and keep it'; Numbers 3:7-8 uses the same pair of verbs for the Levites' tabernacle service. Scholars such as G. K. Beale read Eden as the first sanctuary and Israel as retracing Adam's calling.

How Adam's sin relates to ours has been debated since Augustine, whose Latin Bible read 'in whom all sinned.' The Greek eph' hō is usually rendered 'because.' Traditions differ on inherited guilt, inherited corruption, or representation.
In Matthew 13 the weeds (often identified as darnel) look like wheat until they ripen. The master's patience protects the wheat until harvest.

DEBATES.p: The Hebrew can mean 'like Adam,' 'like mankind,' or refer to the town of Adam (Joshua 3:16), since the verse goes on 'there they have dealt treacherously.' The LSB reads 'like Adam' and tags it as the name; the video builds on that reading.

DEBATES.h: How does Adam's sin reach us?
DEBATES.p: Representation (federal headship, as in the video), natural union with Adam (Augustine), or imitation (Pelagius, rejected by the church). Most Protestant and Catholic traditions hold that humanity is truly implicated in Adam.

DEBATES.h: Does 'all men' in 5:18 mean universal salvation?
DEBATES.p: Most read 'all' as all who are in Christ (compare 'those who receive' in 5:17); a minority read it universally. The video does not address it.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video reads 6:1 as 'that grace may abound'; the LSB has 'so that grace may increase,' and keeps 'abounded all the more' for a different verb in 5:20.

'Israel as a corporate Adam' and the Eden-temple link are scholarly proposals (the video names G. K. Beale) that the video presents as settled; many find them persuasive, but they are interpretations.
'Federal headship' is a later theological term (from Reformed covenant theology), not Paul's own wording.

QUESTIONS: Where do you see Paul 'spiral' back to an earlier theme in Romans 5?
Why does Paul say death reigned even before the Law?
How do Aaron, Achan and the Servant help explain 'one for the many'?
Where are you tempted to treat sin casually because grace abounds?
How does forgetting who reigns change the way believers treat one another?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: Christians live in a world where sin reigns, but they must not live as if sin reigns over them. Romans 6 will make the full case. This is not about perfection; it is about perception. When a Christian acts as if sin still reigns, the distinction that sets them apart blurs and may disappear. One concrete result: God's people begin to relate to one another the way the world does, with suspicion, comparison and judgment rather than mercy and forgiveness. That 'does not come from grace reigning, it comes from forgetting who reigns.' The Roman church showed traces of this in its division and mistrust. Paul wants us to live our faith like we actually believe it is true, and to steward our faith relationship with the Lord thoughtfully and intentionally.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): each morning this week, before checking your phone, say Romans 5:21 aloud and name one way you will live today under the reign of grace.

## The one for the many
1. Romans 5:15; Leviticus 16:17: One for the many
   Paul (Romans 5:15, LSB): "But the gracious gift is not like the transgression. For if by the transgression of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one Man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many."
   Leviticus (Leviticus 16:17, LSB): "Now when he goes in to make atonement in the holy place, no one shall be in the tent of meeting until he comes out, that he may make atonement for himself and for his household and for all the assembly of Israel."

   (video) Paul uses qal vahomer again, as in 5:9-11: if death spread to all through one, much more can God's people rest assured that the grace of Christ leads to righteousness and eternal life.
2. Joshua 7:11; Romans 5:18: 'Israel has sinned'
   Yahweh to Joshua (Joshua 7:11, LSB): "“Israel has sinned, and they have also trespassed against My covenant which I commanded them. And they have even taken some of the things devoted to destruction and have both stolen and dealt falsely. Moreover, they have also put them among their own things."
   Paul (Romans 5:18, LSB): "So then as through one transgression there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness there resulted justification of life to all men."
   (video) Achan stole from the spoils of Jericho, yet God says 'Israel has sinned.' Once again the one stands in for the many. Some today call this federal headship.
   (video) The Servant shows the hopeful side: 'He Himself bore the sin of many' (Isaiah 53:12). (Isaiah 53:11-12)
3. Romans 5:16; Deuteronomy 25:1: Condemnation and justification
   Paul (Romans 5:16, LSB): "And the gift is not like that which came through the one who sinned; for on the one hand the judgment arose from one transgression resulting in condemnation, but on the other hand the gracious gift arose from many transgressions resulting in justification."
   Moses (Deuteronomy 25:1, LSB): "“If there is a dispute between men and they go to court for judgment, and the judges judge their case, and they justify the righteous and condemn the wicked,"
   (video) Justification is God counting a person righteous, not on the basis of their own works but on the basis of the righteousness of Christ (Romans 3:23-25). God did the same in the past: Genesis 15 and Psalm 32. (Romans 3:23-25; Genesis 15:6; Psalm 32:1-2)

## Grace abounded all the more
1. Romans 5:20-21: Grace abounded all the more
   Grace overwhelms sin Romans 5:20-21: "Now the Law came in so that the transgression would increase, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, even so grace would reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Romans+5:20-21
   (video) Notice the different verbs: sin 'increased' (pleonazō), grace 'abounded all the more,' superabounded. Not both getting bigger, but grace decisively overwhelming sin.
   (video) The Law did not force people to sin; it made sin multiply in visibility and accountability so that grace could overwhelm it.
2. Romans 6:1-2; Romans 3:7-8: Are we to continue in sin?
   Paul (Romans 6:1-2, LSB): "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin so that grace may increase? May it never be! How shall we who died to sin still live in it?"
   Paul (Romans 3:8, LSB): "And why not say (as we are slanderously reported and as some claim that we say), “Let us do evil that good may come”? Their condemnation is just."
   (video) Paul spirals back to the objection of chapter 3 because he has just linked increasing sin and abounding grace. He meets the same objection on a deeper level.
   (video) Underneath the 'dumb question' is a casual attitude: if sin and grace live so close together, what's the big deal about sin? Is holiness that important?
3. Matthew 13:29-30: Wheat and weeds together
   Jesus (Matthew 13:29-30, LSB): "But he *said, ‘No; for while you are gathering up the tares, you may uproot the wheat with them. Allow both to grow together until the harvest; and in the time of the harvest I will say to the reapers, “First gather up the tares and bind them in bundles to burn them up; but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”"
   Paul (Romans 5:21, LSB): "so that, as sin reigned in death, even so grace would reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."
   (video) The kingdom of heaven spreads among people beholden to a different kingdom. The parable does not minimize sin; it emphasizes God's patience until the final separation. Those under the reign of grace are constantly surrounded by those under the reign of sin.

## Key people
- Adam: The one man through whom sin and death entered; a type of the One to come. [Background] Paul calls Christ 'the last Adam' in 1 Corinthians 15:45.
- Moses: Death reigned 'until Moses,' when Torah was given at Sinai. [Background] Torah formalized the covenant and its requirements.
- Aaron: The high priest who made atonement for himself and all Israel (Leviticus 16:17). [Background] Brother of Moses and Israel's first high priest.
- Achan: Stole from the spoils of Jericho; God said 'Israel has sinned.' [Background] His story follows the fall of Jericho and explains Israel's defeat at Ai (Joshua 7).
- Hosea: 'like Adam they have trespassed against the covenant' (Hosea 6:7). [Background] An eighth-century prophet to the northern kingdom.
- G. K. Beale: The teacher recommends his book The Temple and the Church's Mission for the Adam-Israel-temple connections. [Background] American New Testament scholar; the book (2004) traces Eden as the first sanctuary.

## Places [Background]
- Jericho (named in the video): Achan took from the things devoted to destruction (Joshua 7).
- Mount Sinai (named in the video): Where the Law came in (Romans 5:20): 'until Moses.' Traditional site.
- Babylon: Israel's exile, which the teacher compares to Adam's expulsion from Eden.

## Key terms
- Reign: Kingly rule. Paul personifies death, sin and grace as kings (Romans 5:14, 17, 21).
- Type: A person or event that prefigures a greater one; Adam is 'a type of Him who was to come' (Romans 5:14).
- Imputed: Counted or charged to someone's account; 'sin is not imputed when there is no law' (Romans 5:13).
- Federal headship: The idea that one representative acts for many, as Adam for humanity and Christ for His people.
- Corporate Adam: The video's term for Israel retracing Adam's vocation and failure (Hosea 6:7).
- Qal vahomer: Lesser-to-greater argument: if one man's sin did this, much more will Christ's grace (Romans 5:15, 17).
- Condemnation: The judge's verdict of guilty and its sentence; the opposite of justification (Romans 5:16, 18).

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Paul's spiral: The video describes Paul's style as Hebraic and spiral: he returns to sin, Law and grace again and again, each time with a new purpose. Ancient writers often used repetition and ring structure to build an argument.
- Adam and Israel: Genesis 2:15 says the man was set in the garden 'to cultivate it and keep it'; Numbers 3:7-8 uses the same pair of verbs for the Levites' tabernacle service. Scholars such as G. K. Beale read Eden as the first sanctuary and Israel as retracing Adam's calling.
- 'Because all sinned' (5:12): How Adam's sin relates to ours has been debated since Augustine, whose Latin Bible read 'in whom all sinned.' The Greek eph' hō is usually rendered 'because.' Traditions differ on inherited guilt, inherited corruption, or representation.
- Wheat and weeds: In Matthew 13 the weeds (often identified as darnel) look like wheat until they ripen. The master's patience protects the wheat until harvest.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Hosea 6:7: 'like Adam'? The Hebrew can mean 'like Adam,' 'like mankind,' or refer to the town of Adam (Joshua 3:16), since the verse goes on 'there they have dealt treacherously.' The LSB reads 'like Adam' and tags it as the name; the video builds on that reading.
- How does Adam's sin reach us? Representation (federal headship, as in the video), natural union with Adam (Augustine), or imitation (Pelagius, rejected by the church). Most Protestant and Catholic traditions hold that humanity is truly implicated in Adam.
- Does 'all men' in 5:18 mean universal salvation? Most read 'all' as all who are in Christ (compare 'those who receive' in 5:17); a minority read it universally. The video does not address it.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video reads 6:1 as 'that grace may abound'; the LSB has 'so that grace may increase,' and keeps 'abounded all the more' for a different verb in 5:20.
- 'Israel as a corporate Adam' and the Eden-temple link are scholarly proposals (the video names G. K. Beale) that the video presents as settled; many find them persuasive, but they are interpretations.
- 'Federal headship' is a later theological term (from Reformed covenant theology), not Paul's own wording.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Where do you see Paul 'spiral' back to an earlier theme in Romans 5?
2. Why does Paul say death reigned even before the Law?
3. How do Aaron, Achan and the Servant help explain 'one for the many'?
4. Where are you tempted to treat sin casually because grace abounds?
5. How does forgetting who reigns change the way believers treat one another?

## Application
- (video) Christians live in a world where sin reigns, but they must not live as if sin reigns over them. Romans 6 will make the full case. This is not about perfection; it is about perception. When a Christian acts as if sin still reigns, the distinction that sets them apart blurs and may disappear. One concrete result: God's people begin to relate to one another the way the world does, with suspicion, comparison and judgment rather than mercy and forgiveness. That 'does not come from grace reigning, it comes from forgetting who reigns.' The Roman church showed traces of this in its division and mistrust. Paul wants us to live our faith like we actually believe it is true, and to steward our faith relationship with the Lord thoughtfully and intentionally.
- Study note (added): each morning this week, before checking your phone, say Romans 5:21 aloud and name one way you will live today under the reign of grace.
